chief_complaint: sudden, profound, painless loss of vision in one eye with cherry-red spot on fundus exam (Central Retinal Artery Occlusion)
hpi_details: 71M with history of carotid stenosis and atrial fibrillation suddenly experienced complete, painless loss of vision in his left eye 2 hours ago while reading the newspaper. Describes vision dropping instantly 'like turning off a light switch' to complete darkness/light perception only. Denies eye pain, headache, jaw claudication, or scalp tenderness.
ideas: shocked and terrified by abrupt total blindness in left eye
concerns: thinks he suffered an eye stroke or blood clot
expectations: wants immediate emergency intervention to restore blood flow before his vision is lost forever
pmh: Atrial Fibrillation (off anticoagulation), Left Internal Carotid Artery 70% stenosis, Hypertension

investigation_events.title: Emergency dilated fundus examination
investigation_events.availability_message: The emergency fundus result is now available. Stroke-center transfer must not be delayed.

results.value: Diffuse retinal whitening with attenuated segmented arterioles and a central cherry-red spot
results.note: Consistent with central retinal artery occlusion.

clinical_knowledge.topic: Central retinal artery occlusion (CRAO) evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Central retinal artery occlusion (CRAO) is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.
Standard management emphasizes immediate emergency-stroke-center evaluation and secondary prevention, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: sudden, profound, painless loss of vision in one eye with cherry-red spot on fundus exam (Central Retinal Artery Occlusion)

Key HPI features: 71M with history of carotid stenosis and atrial fibrillation suddenly experienced complete, painless loss of vision in his left eye 2 hours ago while reading the newspaper. Describes vision dropping instantly 'like turning off a light switch' to complete darkness/light perception only. Denies eye pain, headache, jaw claudication, or scalp tenderness.

Objective/Exam findings: Vitals: HR 88 (irregularly irregular), BP 162/96. Visual acuity: Left eye Light Perception (LP) only; Right eye 20/30. Left eye pupil exhibits a dense Relative Afferent Pupillary Defect (RAPD). Slit-lamp anterior segment normal. Dilated funduscopic examination of the left eye reveals diffuse, pale, opaque whitening of the entire neurosensory retina (retinal edema/ischemia) with attenuation and segmentation of retinal arterioles ('box-carring' / cattle-trucking of blood column). At the fovea, where the inner retina is thin, the underlying choroidal circulation shines through brightly, creating the classic pathognomonic 'Cherry-Red Spot'. No temporal artery tenderness; ESR/CRP normal.
Relevant background/PMH: Atrial Fibrillation (off anticoagulation), Left Internal Carotid Artery 70% stenosis, Hypertension
Current medications: Metoprolol 50mg BID, Aspirin 81mg daily
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Central retinal artery occlusion (CRAO).
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Giant cell arteritis (arteritic CRAO) without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Sudden painless complete monocular blindness.
management_principles: Treat as an acute ischemic stroke: immediately transfer to the nearest emergency stroke center for coordinated ophthalmology and neurology evaluation

Obtain urgent stroke evaluation and assess for arteritic CRAO (including ESR, CRP, and platelet count when clinically indicated); start high-dose systemic corticosteroids immediately if giant cell arteritis is suspected
Conservative ocular maneuvers such as ocular massage, anterior-chamber paracentesis, and IOP-lowering treatment have not shown benefit and should not delay stroke-center evaluation
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: 71M vasculopathic patient presenting within 2 hours of sudden, catastrophic, painless monocular visual loss pathognomonic for Central Retinal Artery Occlusion (CRAO).
reference_soap.objective: Vitals: HR 88 (irregularly irregular), BP 162/96. Visual acuity: Left eye Light Perception (LP) only; Right eye 20/30. Left eye pupil exhibits a dense Relative Afferent Pupillary Defect (RAPD). Slit-lamp anterior segment normal. Dilated funduscopic examination of the left eye reveals diffuse, pale, opaque whitening of the entire neurosensory retina (retinal edema/ischemia) with attenuation and segmentation of retinal arterioles ('box-carring' / cattle-trucking of blood column). At the fovea, where the inner retina is thin, the underlying choroidal circulation shines through brightly, creating the classic pathognomonic 'Cherry-Red Spot'. No temporal artery tenderness; ESR/CRP normal.
reference_soap.assessment: Acute Central Retinal Artery Occlusion (CRAO - Ocular Stroke / Retinal Infarction) secondary to thromboembolism from carotid artery or atrial fibrillation.
reference_soap.plan: Treat as an acute ischemic stroke with immediate transfer to the nearest emergency stroke center for coordinated ophthalmology and neurology evaluation. Obtain urgent vascular and cardioembolic evaluation and assess for giant cell arteritis (including ESR, CRP, and platelet count when clinically indicated); begin high-dose systemic corticosteroids immediately if giant cell arteritis is suspected. Conservative ocular maneuvers, including ocular massage, anterior-chamber paracentesis, IOP-lowering therapy, and hypercapnia techniques, have not shown benefit and should not delay stroke evaluation. Consider thrombolysis only through the stroke team for a patient who meets systemic eligibility criteria.

learning_objectives: Recognize Central Retinal Artery Occlusion (CRAO) as a true ocular stroke presenting with sudden, profound, painless monocular blindness and positive RAPD
Interpret pathognomonic funduscopic features of CRAO (diffuse retinal ischemic whitening, attenuated box-carring arterioles, and foveal Cherry-Red Spot)
Treat CRAO as an acute ischemic stroke requiring immediate stroke-center evaluation, vascular risk assessment, and secondary prevention
Differentiate thromboembolic CRAO from Giant Cell Arteritis (arteritic CRAO) which requires immediate high-dose IV methylprednisolone to prevent contralateral blindness

teaching.one_liner: 71M with AFib and carotid stenosis with sudden painless complete vision loss in one eye, like a light switch turning off.
red_flags: History of AFib or carotid disease

must_ask.say: Exactly what time did your vision go dark? This is critical for treatment.
Is there any pain, and can you see anything at all, such as light or shapes?

must_ask.objective: Screen for giant cell arteritis symptoms
must_ask.say: Do you have any scalp tenderness, jaw pain when chewing, or headaches?
Do you have atrial fibrillation or carotid artery disease?
This may be an eye stroke, so we need immediate emergency stroke-center evaluation; every minute counts.

history.answer: About two hours ago, my left eye suddenly went completely black while I was sitting down reading the newspaper.
It happened all at once two hours ago. It was not gradual at all; it was just like somebody flipped a light switch off.
It is only in my left eye. When I close my left eye, my right eye sees perfectly fine.
No, it has stayed completely dark for the past two hours without any improvement or clearing.
The entire vision in that eye is gone; everything is pitch black, and I can barely tell if a bright light is shining.
I cannot see anything near or far with my left eye. I have not changed my reading glasses recently.
No, I have not had any glare, halos around streetlights, or trouble driving at night before this happened.
No, I never saw any flashes of light, floating spots, or a dark curtain falling over the eye.
No, I have not experienced double vision at all.
No, my eyelids are not drooping, and I have no weakness or trouble chewing and swallowing.
No, there is no pain whatsoever, no discomfort when moving my eye, and no redness.
No, I have not had any new headaches, and my scalp or temples are not tender when I touch them.
No, I do not have any jaw pain or fatigue when chewing, and no stiffness in my neck or shoulders.
No, I have no weakness or numbness in my arms or legs, my speech is normal, and I am not dizzy.
No, I have not hit my head or injured my eye in any way.
I have had high blood pressure for about ten years and take pills for it. I do not have diabetes, and my last eye exam was two years ago.
I have an irregular heart rhythm called atrial fibrillation, and the doctors also found a seventy percent blockage in my left carotid artery.
No, I do not have severe nearsightedness or glaucoma, and I have never had cataract surgery or any other eye operation.
No, I have never taken oral steroids, hydroxychloroquine, or tuberculosis medications.
No one in my family has had glaucoma, macular degeneration, or sudden loss of vision.
I had to stop reading immediately, and I certainly cannot drive or walk around safely like this, though I have not fallen.
I am terrified that a blood clot broke loose and caused a stroke in my eye.
I know time is critical; I want emergency treatment right away to restore blood flow before the vision is lost permanently.
Aside from my high blood pressure, irregular heartbeat, and neck artery blockage, I have been in good health.
I stayed in the hospital a couple of years ago when they found the atrial fibrillation and carotid blockage, but I have never had surgery.
I take metoprolol fifty milligrams twice a day and baby aspirin eighty-one milligrams daily. I was taken off my stronger blood thinner a while ago.
No, I do not have any allergies to medications.
I have never smoked cigarettes in my life.
I rarely drink alcohol, perhaps just a glass of wine on a special holiday.
I am a retired electrical engineer, and I live at home with my wife.
My father had high blood pressure and passed away from a stroke in his seventies, but there are no other major illnesses in the family.

exam.finding: Blood pressure is 162/96 mmHg, pulse is 88 beats per minute and irregularly irregular, respiratory rate is 16 breaths per minute, body temperature is 36.7°C, and oxygen saturation is 98% on room air.
Elderly male appearing alert and visibly distressed regarding sudden left eye vision loss, without outward signs of acute trauma.
Conjunctivae are clear without injection, pallor, or discharge; sclerae are anicteric bilaterally.

Visual acuity is 20/30 in the right eye and light perception only in the left; left pupil demonstrates a dense relative afferent pupillary defect, and left funduscopy shows diffuse retinal whitening with arteriolar box-carring and a cherry-red spot at the fovea.
Temporal arteries are pulsatile without tenderness, thickening, or nodularity bilaterally.
Heart rhythm is irregularly irregular with normal first and second heart sounds, and no audible murmurs, rubs, or gallops.
Extraocular movements are intact without nystagmus or ptosis, facial sensation and expression are symmetric, and lower cranial nerves are intact.
Motor strength is 5/5 in all four extremities symmetrically with normal muscle tone and no pronator drift.
